properties.decision:
Recorded as BRAINSTORMING, not as a proposal. Anthony, 2026-09-06, in his words: "as we've gone through this design process, it seems that we continue to make more rules and more rules. wondering if there is a way to measure if a set of rules will eventually converge on a finite set of design nodes/edges or if by adding another rule, we will eventually have to add another ruleset to counter something false about a previously implemented node/edge. if so, will this continue to grow and grow? in some ways, I feel like it a decision tree that continues to fork and fork because we have some new information that requires a nuanced offshoot of a previous decision. just curious if there is some graph theory operation or mathematical proof about if something continues to grow/bloom or if it will converge to some finite set of rules that the design can actually implement … mostly me musing about if we'll ever conclude the reflow2 design implementation and more generally speaking, if any reflow2 design can be assured of closure?"

TWO QUESTIONS INSIDE IT, and they have different answers:
Q1 — the RULESET of reflow2's own development: does it converge?
Q2 — the CLOSURE of a design held in reflow2: can any design reach a state where the loop owes nothing, and can that be assured?

THE FRAMINGS, as they separate (none is a decision):

(a) FIXED POINTS OVER A LATTICE (Tarski / Kleene). If every rule only ADDS structure (draw the missing edge, add the missing node) and the universe is finite, iterating a monotone operator converges to a least fixed point — that is a theorem. Counter-argument: the rules here are NOT monotone. Anthony's own description — "add another ruleset to counter something false about a previously implemented node/edge" — is non-monotonic revision (default logic, AGM belief revision), and no convergence theorem exists there in general. The measured shape agrees: 12 of this design's 26 DesignRules cite another rule in their own text, and 7 name a defect, a skipped step or a failure as the reason they exist — rules about rules are half the population.

(b) UNDECIDABILITY (Rice / Gödel-shaped). The rules are about BEHAVIOUR of a system, and "does this ruleset need no further rule" is a non-trivial semantic property of that system — undecidable in general. So NO proof of closure can exist for an open-world design. Counter-argument: undecidable in general is not unmeasurable in particular; a specific process can be shown convergent by a potential function even when the general question has no decision procedure. This is the honest limit, not a reason to stop measuring.

(c) REQUISITE VARIETY (Ashby). A regulator's rules must match the variety of what it regulates. reflow2's rules grow because USAGE supplies new variety — nearly every rule of the last month was set from a field report or a session's own failure. On this reading Q1's answer is: the ruleset converges exactly when the user population stops producing new kinds of failure — closure is a property of the environment, not of the graph. Counter-argument: that makes "will it ever conclude" answerable only in hindsight; but it also names the measurement — rules per unit of NEW usage, not rules per week.

(d) SOFTWARE RELIABILITY GROWTH (Goel–Okumoto and kin). For a FIXED scope, defects found over time follow a saturating curve, and the curve's asymptote is estimable from the data. Measured here: defect facts recorded 126 in August, 26 in the first six days of September — about 4.1/day then 4.3/day. FLAT, NOT SATURATING. Rules: 3 in July, 18 in August, 5 in six days of September — also not decelerating. Counter-argument: the scope is not fixed (four items shipped this week), so the curve is for a moving target and says only that discovery has not slowed, not that it will not.

(e) THE DECISION TREE THAT FORKS. Anthony's picture: each nuance is an offshoot of a prior decision. Structurally the graph disagrees with the picture — only 17 Decision→Decision SUPERSEDES/EVOLVES_INTO edges among 632 Decisions — so the forks live in PROSE (a decision's text saying "distinct from X, which decided Y") rather than as edges, and the tree's branching factor cannot be computed today. Counter-argument: that is itself a finding; if the forks were edges, the branching factor and the leaf-closure rate (forks that end in an accepted ruling vs forks that breed another fork) would be a one-line query, and that ratio is the convergence measure Anthony is asking for.

(f) CLOSURE OF A USER'S DESIGN AS A WELL-FOUNDED LOOP (Q2). Define closure as: every detector silent at a fixed scope. That is a fixed point of the detect→answer operator, and it is reachable IF the detector set is WELL-FOUNDED — every honest answer to a gap strictly decreases some potential Φ(design) and creates no new gap. Today it is NOT: fact:defect-one-missing-edge-arrives-as-three-findings records that one answer can raise three findings, and adding a Capability to answer one gap raises unallocated/unrealized/unverified gaps of its own. Counter-argument on the other side: that is a DESIGNABLE property of the 49 detectors, not a law — a test could drive a random design through "answer every gap with its minimal honest answer" and assert termination, and a detector whose answer can raise a gap of the same kind is the one to fix. Cheap to attempt; the theorem would be reflow2's, about its own detectors, and would say nothing about whether the user's INTENT is finished.

WHAT IS CHEAP: (d) and (e) are one-line measurements on the export and are already partly taken above; (f) is one property test. WHAT IS EXPENSIVE: any general proof — (b) says there is none.
properties.name: OPEN — does the ruleset converge on a finite set of design nodes and edges, or does each rule breed the next? Is closure of a reflow2 design (this one, or any) provable, or only measurable?
properties.rationale: A RANKING IS A FINDING, NOT A DECISION. The honest answer to "can any reflow2 design be assured of closure" is NO in the general case (b) and YES for a narrower thing worth having (f): closure of the LOOP over a fixed scope is a well-foundedness property of the detector set, provable per detector set and testable today, whereas closure of INTENT is bounded by the variety of the world the design meets (c) and is only ever measured in hindsight (d). For Q1 the useful instrument is not "are rules still being added" but "what fraction of new rules exist to correct a prior rule" (12 of 26 now) and "rules per unit of new usage" — a ruleset that only grows when the world shows it something new is regulating, not blooming; one that grows to patch its own last rule is the divergent case Anthony fears. Related open question dec:idea-silence-is-reported-not-inferred asked the same thing one level down: whether to add a detector per blind spot or make "I could not see this" a reportable state — the detector count (49) is the ruleset's mechanical twin and has the same growth question. Nothing here is proposed for building; the one thing that would turn this from musing into an instrument is drawing the forks as edges (e) so the tree can be measured. Anthony's call whether any of it is worth a session.
